def: The money obtained from working or from investing capital.
ex: The software company reported record quarterly earnings during the investor conference call.
nat: Inflation has significantly reduced average real earnings this year.

mis.bad: He invested all his earning in stocks.
mis.good: He invested all his earnings in stocks.
mis.why: "Earnings" is always plural when referring to income or company profits.

def: Unconventional and slightly strange in behavior or appearance.
ex: Our lead architect has an eccentric habit of coding only late at night.
nat: His eccentric wardrobe always attracted attention at design conferences.

mis.bad: He is an eccentric person about his food.
mis.good: He is very eccentric about his food.
mis.why: Use "eccentric about" or simply describe the behavior without redundant words.

def: To repeat sound by reflection, or closely imitate or reflect an idea.
ex: Her thoughtful recommendations echoed throughout the executive boardroom during the entire meeting.
nat: The loud footsteps echoed in the empty corridor.

mis.bad: The sound echoed on the walls of the room.
mis.good: The sound echoed off the walls of the room.
mis.why: Sound echoes "off" or "around" a surface or space, not "on".

def: To obscure the light from, or surpass in importance or prominence.
ex: The new smartphone launch will easily eclipse all previous sales milestones this quarter.
nat: Her athletic achievements eventually eclipsed those of her older sister.

mis.bad: The news eclipsed all other informations today.
mis.good: The news eclipsed all other news today.
mis.why: "Information" is uncountable in English; use "other news" or "pieces of information".

def: Giving good value or return in relation to money, time, or effort spent.
ex: Riding a bicycle to the office is both healthy and highly economical.
nat: Electric heat pumps provide an economical way to warm your home.

mis.bad: This hybrid car is very economic on fuel.
mis.good: This hybrid car is very economical on fuel.
mis.why: False friend! "Economic" relates to the economy; "economical" means saving money or resources.

def: An advantage over competitors, or the outside limit of an object.
ex: Fluent English gives job candidates a distinct competitive edge in international tech interviews.
nat: Be careful not to leave your glass near the table edge.

mis.bad: Our company has an edge above other competitors.
mis.good: Our company has an edge over other competitors.
mis.why: Use the preposition "over" with "edge" when expressing an advantage over someone.

def: Fit or suitable to be eaten; not toxic or poisonous.
ex: Only collect wild mushrooms if you are completely certain that they are edible.
nat: The cake was decorated with delicate edible flowers.

mis.bad: Are these berries eatable or toxic?
mis.good: Are these berries edible or toxic?
mis.why: While "eatable" exists, "edible" is the standard word for safe to consume.

def: Strange and frightening; suggesting supernatural influence.
ex: An eerie silence settled over the deserted train platform late at night.
nat: The abandoned factory looked eerie under the pale moonlight.

mis.bad: The street was with an eerie atmosphere.
mis.good: The street had an eerie atmosphere.
mis.why: Use "had an eerie atmosphere" rather than "was with".

def: Successful in producing a desired or intended result.
ex: Regular spaced repetition is an effective technique for memorizing long vocabulary lists.
nat: The new security policy proved effective within its first month.

mis.bad: This medicine was very efficient for my headache.
mis.good: This medicine was very effective for my headache.
mis.why: "Effective" means achieving the desired result; "efficient" means doing it without wasting time/effort.

def: Requiring no physical or mental exertion; achieved with admirable ease.
ex: Her presentation flowed so smoothly that speaking in public seemed completely effortless.
nat: With enough practice, switching keyboard shortcuts becomes almost effortless.

mis.bad: He made the speech look very effortlessly.
mis.good: He made the speech look very effortless.
mis.why: After linking verbs like "look" or "seem", use the adjective "effortless", not an adverb.

def: A person's sense of self-esteem or self-importance.
ex: A good team leader keeps personal ego out of technical architecture debates.
nat: Criticism can damage a junior developer's fragile ego.

mis.bad: He has a very big egoism.
mis.good: He has a very big ego.
mis.why: "Egoism" is philosophical selfishness; use "ego" for self-esteem or pride.

def: Able to resume normal shape after contraction or distortion; flexible and adaptable.
ex: Cloud computing allows companies to scale servers quickly using an elastic infrastructure model.
nat: The waist of these running pants is made from elastic fabric.

mis.bad: Our budget needs to be plastic for changes.
mis.good: Our budget needs to be elastic / flexible for changes.
mis.why: Do not say "plastic" for flexibility in English; use "elastic" or "flexible".

def: A polite word for people who are old.
ex: Volunteers delivered warm meals to elderly residents who could not leave their homes.
nat: The bus driver waited patiently for the elderly passenger to sit down.

mis.bad: There were several elderlies waiting in the clinic.
mis.good: There were several elderly people waiting in the clinic.
mis.why: "Elderly" is an adjective; use "elderly people" or "the elderly", not "elderlies".

def: Pleasingly graceful and stylish in appearance or manner; ingeniously simple.
ex: The software architect designed an elegant solution that required only twenty lines of code.
nat: She wore an elegant dark suit to the final interview.

mis.bad: She solved the bug very elegant.
mis.good: She solved the bug very elegantly.
mis.why: Use the adverb "elegantly" to modify verbs.

def: An essential or characteristic part of something abstract or physical.
ex: Clear communication between team members is a vital element of any successful project.
nat: Phosphorus is a chemical element essential for cellular energy.

mis.bad: Trust is an important element from a good relationship.
mis.good: Trust is an important element of a good relationship.
mis.why: Use "element of", not "element from".

def: To raise to a more important or higher status, level, or position.
ex: Completing high-profile cloud projects helped elevate her standing within the global organization.
nat: Regular cardio exercise will elevate your heart rate safely.

mis.bad: The manager elevated him for senior engineer.
mis.good: The manager elevated him to senior engineer.
mis.why: Use "elevate to [a title or rank]", not "for".

def: Having the right qualifications or satisfying the necessary conditions.
ex: Employees who complete six months of service become eligible for annual bonus payments.
nat: Only registered voters are eligible to participate in the primary election.

mis.bad: He is eligible to the promotion after one year.
mis.good: He is eligible for the promotion after one year.
mis.why: Use "eligible for + noun" and "eligible to + verb".

def: To completely remove or get rid of something undesirable.
ex: Automating the data pipeline will eliminate manual entry errors across our billing system.
nat: The team was eliminated in the tournament semi-finals.

mis.bad: We need to eliminate of these unnecessary meetings.
mis.good: We need to eliminate these unnecessary meetings.
mis.why: "Eliminate" is transitive; do not insert "of" after it.

def: Representing the best, highest-ranking, or most powerful group of people.
ex: The company recruited elite software engineers from top universities around the world.
nat: Elite marathon runners maintain an astonishing pace throughout the entire race.

mis.bad: He belongs to an elitist group of scientists.
mis.good: He belongs to an elite group of scientists.
mis.why: "Elitist" carries a negative snobbish tone; "elite" simply means top-ranking or highest quality.

def: Fluent or persuasive in speaking or writing clearly and expressively.
ex: The young lawyer gave an eloquent closing argument that deeply moved the jury.
nat: Her silence was an eloquent reminder of how disappointed she felt.

mis.bad: He made an eloquent speech with many words.
mis.good: He gave an eloquent speech.
mis.why: Say "give a speech" rather than "make a speech", and avoid redundancy with "eloquent".

pt: esquivo / difícil de capturar ou definir
def: Difficult to find, catch, achieve, or remember clearly.
ex: Finding an elusive race condition bug took the senior engineering team several days.
nat: True work-life balance often remains elusive for startup founders.

mis.bad: The solution remained elusive for our entire team.
mis.good: The solution remained elusive to our entire team.
mis.why: Use "elusive to [someone]", not "for".

def: An official ban on trade or other commercial activity with a particular country.
ex: Several European nations placed a strict trade embargo on the hostile foreign regime.
nat: The publication embargo lifts tomorrow morning at eight o'clock sharp.

mis.bad: The government put an embargo in imports.
mis.good: The government placed an embargo on imports.
mis.why: Use the collocation "place an embargo on", not "put an embargo in".

def: To accept or support a belief, theory, or change willingly and enthusiastically.
ex: Modern tech companies must embrace remote work to attract the best global talent.
nat: The two friends embraced warmly at the arrivals gate.

mis.bad: Our company must embrace to the digital transformation.
mis.good: Our company must embrace digital transformation.
mis.why: "Embrace" is transitive; do not place "to" after the verb.

def: Famous and respected within a particular sphere, profession, or discipline.
ex: The keynote address was delivered by an eminent professor of artificial intelligence.
nat: She studied under an eminent neurosurgeon at Johns Hopkins Hospital.

mis.bad: The collapse of the bridge was eminent.
mis.good: The collapse of the bridge was imminent.
mis.why: Do not confuse "eminent" (distinguished) with "imminent" (about to happen).

def: To discharge or produce something such as gas, radiation, or sound.
ex: Older diesel buses emit significantly more harmful particles than modern electric vehicles.
nat: The device will emit a high-pitched beep when battery voltage drops.

mis.bad: The engine emits out dangerous fumes.
mis.good: The engine emits dangerous fumes.
mis.why: Do not add "out" after "emit"; the verb already implies outward release.

def: A strong feeling deriving from one's circumstances, mood, or relationships with others.
ex: His trembling voice was filled with deep emotion as he thanked his parents.
nat: It is normal to experience a wide range of emotions during difficult transitions.

mis.bad: He could not control his emotion during the speech.
mis.good: He could not control his emotions during the speech.
mis.why: When referring to someone's internal feelings in general, use the plural "emotions".

def: Relating to a person's feelings or the expression of feelings.
ex: Moving to a new country was an emotional journey for our whole family.
nat: She offered valuable emotional support while I recovered from surgery.

mis.bad: I felt very emotional with the ending of the book.
mis.good: I felt very emotional about / at the ending of the book.
mis.why: Use "emotional about" or "emotional at", not "with".

def: To give someone the authority or means to do something; make possible.
ex: This new software update will enable remote teams to collaborate seamlessly in real time.
nat: Two-factor authentication enables users to protect their accounts against fraud.

mis.bad: This tool enables to export files to PDF.
mis.good: This tool enables users to export files to PDF.
mis.why: "Enable" requires a direct object: "enable [someone] to [do something]".

def: To make a bill or proposal into law; or put into practice.
ex: Parliament voted overwhelmingly to enact strict regulations on artificial intelligence consumer products.
nat: The school board enacted a comprehensive anti-bullying policy last semester.

mis.bad: The government enacted to a new privacy law.
mis.good: The government enacted a new privacy law.
mis.why: "Enact" is a transitive verb; omit "to".

def: To fill someone with great delight or charm; or put under a magical spell.
ex: The historic architecture of the ancient capital will enchant visitors from every nation.
nat: Her lovely singing voice enchanted the entire audience last night.

mis.bad: I was very enchanted with the old town.
mis.good: I was enchanted by the old town.
mis.why: Use the preposition "by" when passive: "enchanted by something".

def: To surround on all sides, or place something inside an envelope or package.
ex: Please sign the contract and return it in the enclosed postage-paid envelope.
nat: A high wooden fence encloses the private garden behind the house.

mis.bad: Please find enclose my resume for your review.
mis.good: Please find enclosed my resume for your review.
mis.why: Use the past participle "enclosed" in the standard business formula "Please find enclosed".

def: To include or contain a wide range of things or ideas.
ex: The computer science curriculum will encompass machine learning, cybersecurity, and cloud architecture.
nat: Her duties encompass managing client relationships and overseeing product development.

mis.bad: The training encompasses about five different programming languages.
mis.good: The training encompasses five different programming languages.
mis.why: "Encompass" is transitive and does not take "about".

def: To unexpectedly experience or be faced with something difficult or hostile.
ex: Software developers frequently encounter mysterious bugs when migrating code to new cloud platforms.
nat: We encountered severe turbulence during our flight across the Andes.

mis.bad: I encountered with an error while downloading the file.
mis.good: I encountered an error while downloading the file.
mis.why: "Encounter" is transitive in English; do not add "with".

def: To give support, confidence, or hope to someone.
ex: Our engineering manager always encourages developers to learn new tools and frameworks.
nat: Her parents encouraged her to pursue a career in aerospace engineering.

mis.bad: My manager encouraged me doing the English course.
mis.good: My manager encouraged me to do the English course.
mis.why: Use the pattern "encourage someone to + base verb", not "-ing".

def: An attempt to achieve a goal; earnest and conscientious effort.
ex: Launching an electric vehicle startup is an expensive and complex technological endeavor.
nat: We wish you every success in all your future artistic endeavors.

mis.bad: We made an endeavor for finish before Friday.
mis.good: We made an endeavor to finish before Friday.
mis.why: Use "endeavor to + base verb", not "for + verb".

def: To provide with a quality, ability, or asset, or establish with funds.
ex: The prestigious tech university was generously endowed by several prominent Silicon Valley entrepreneurs.
nat: Nature has endowed the region with breathtaking scenic beauty.

mis.bad: He was endowed of extraordinary mathematical talent.
mis.good: He was endowed with extraordinary mathematical talent.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "with" after "endowed": "endowed with [talent/wealth]".

def: To suffer patiently something painful or difficult, or remain in existence.
ex: Passengers had to endure four hours of delays during the sudden airport power outage.
nat: Their friendship has endured through thirty years of changing circumstances.

mis.bad: I cannot endure with this continuous loud drilling.
mis.good: I cannot endure this continuous loud drilling.
mis.why: "Endure" is a transitive verb; do not add "with" after it.

def: Showing or involving great activity, enthusiasm, or vitality.
ex: The fitness trainer led an energetic morning workout that motivated the entire group.
nat: Puppies are naturally energetic and need plenty of space to run.

mis.bad: He is an energic worker who never slows down.
mis.good: He is an energetic worker who never slows down.
mis.why: The standard English adjective is "energetic", not "energic".

def: A machine with moving parts that converts power into motion, or software engine.
ex: The aircraft maintenance crew checked the left jet engine thoroughly before departure.
nat: Google developed a powerful search engine to index internet websites.

mis.bad: The car has a motor problem under the hood.
mis.good: The car has engine trouble under the hood.
mis.why: In vehicles, the internal combustion power unit is called an "engine", while "motor" is usually electric.

def: Having all one's attention or interest absorbed by someone or something.
ex: She was so engrossed in her programming tutorial that she missed dinner completely.
nat: He sat quietly by the window, engrossed in a mystery novel.

mis.bad: He was engrossed on his phone during the lecture.
mis.good: He was engrossed in his phone / book during the lecture.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "in" with "engrossed": "engrossed in something".

def: A person or thing that is mysterious, puzzling, or difficult to understand.
ex: Why the production database suddenly restarted without any logged errors remains an enigma.
nat: The mysterious painting has been an enigma to art historians for centuries.

mis.bad: His sudden resignation is an enigma for our team.
mis.good: His sudden resignation is an enigma to our team.
mis.why: Use "an enigma to [someone]", not "for".

def: Giving delight or pleasure; satisfying.
ex: We spent a thoroughly enjoyable weekend hiking through the national park with friends.
nat: Learning a language should be an enjoyable experience rather than a stressful chore.

mis.bad: The trip was very much enjoyable to all.
mis.good: The trip was very enjoyable for all of us.
mis.why: Say "very enjoyable", not "very much enjoyable", and use "for all of us".

def: To make or become bigger or more extensive in size.
ex: Click on the thumbnail if you wish to enlarge the diagram on screen.
nat: The hospital plans to enlarge its emergency department next year.

mis.bad: Can you enlarge the font more bigger?
mis.good: Can you enlarge the font? / make the font bigger?
mis.why: Do not say "enlarge more bigger"; "enlarge" already means make bigger.

def: To give greater knowledge and understanding about a subject or situation.
ex: Could someone please enlighten our team on why this architectural change was approved?
nat: The documentary will enlighten viewers about marine ecosystem conservation.

mis.bad: Could you enlighten to me about this decision?
mis.good: Could you enlighten me on / about this decision?
mis.why: "Enlighten" takes a direct personal object without "to": "enlighten me".

def: Very large in size, quantity, or extent.
ex: The construction of the new high-speed rail line requires an enormous financial investment.
nat: She felt an enormous sense of relief when the surgery ended successfully.

mis.bad: It was an enormous big challenge for the team.
mis.good: It was an enormous challenge for the team.
mis.why: Never say "enormous big"; "enormous" is an extreme adjective that already means very big.

def: To improve or enhance the quality or value of something.
ex: Living in another country for a year will enrich your cultural perspective immensely.
nat: Organic compost is used by farmers to enrich depleted agricultural soil.

mis.bad: Reading books enriches of your knowledge.
mis.good: Reading books enriches your knowledge.
mis.why: "Enrich" is a transitive verb; do not add "of" after it.

def: To make certain that something will occur or be so.
ex: Please run all automated unit tests before merging to ensure nothing is broken.
nat: Safety harnesses ensure the security of high-rise construction workers.

mis.bad: We need to ensure of the quality of code.
mis.good: We need to ensure the quality of the code.
mis.why: "Ensure" takes a direct object or a "that" clause, never "of".

def: A project or undertaking, typically one that is difficult or requires effort; or a large business.
ex: Our cloud software platform is designed specifically for large enterprise customers across banking.
nat: Starting a business in a foreign country is a daring commercial enterprise.

mis.bad: He opened a small enterprise in his neighborhood.
mis.good: He opened a small business in his neighborhood.
mis.why: In business, "enterprise" usually implies a large corporate scale; use "small business" for small shops.

def: To provide someone with amusement, or give attention and consideration to an idea.
ex: The board of directors refused to entertain any buyout offers from aggressive foreign competitors.
nat: Comedians entertained the guests during the annual charity dinner.

mis.bad: The clown entertained to all the children.
mis.good: The clown entertained all the children.
mis.why: "Entertain" is transitive; do not place "to" before the audience.

def: A thing with distinct and independent existence in business, law, or philosophy.
ex: The company established a separate legal entity to handle its international cloud operations.
nat: Each department operates as a semi-autonomous financial entity within the university.

mis.bad: The branch is an independent entity from the parent.
mis.good: The branch is an independent entity separate from the parent.
mis.why: Say "an independent entity" or "separate from", rather than "independent entity from".

def: To give someone a legal right or a just claim to receive or do something.
ex: Your monthly premium membership will entitle you to unlimited access to our audio courses.
nat: The author entitled her memoir after a line from Shakespeare.

mis.bad: This voucher entitles to get a free coffee.
mis.good: This voucher entitles you to get a free coffee.
mis.why: "Entitle" needs a personal object: "entitle [someone] to [something]".

def: An opening or passage through which someone enters a building, room, or space.
ex: Please gather near the main entrance of the conference center at nine o'clock.
nat: The grand entrance to the palace was decorated with polished marble columns.

mis.bad: The entrance for the subway is across the street.
mis.good: The entrance to the subway is across the street.
mis.why: Use the preposition "to" after "entrance", not "for".

def: An act of going or coming in; or an item written in a list, diary, or database.
ex: Our system generates a detailed audit entry whenever a database record is modified.
nat: Entry into the competition is open to all university undergraduate students.

mis.bad: The entry to the museum is free on Sundays.
mis.good: Entry to / into the museum is free on Sundays.
mis.why: Use "entry to" or "entry into" without the definite article when meaning permission to enter.

def: A flat paper container with a sealable flap, used for enclosing a letter or document.
ex: She sealed the handwritten letter inside a white envelope and stamped it carefully.
nat: The courier handed over a thick sealed envelope containing legal contracts.

mis.bad: Put the document inside of the envelope.
mis.good: Put the document inside the envelope.
mis.why: Avoid the informal redundant "inside of"; simply say "inside the envelope".

def: To imagine as a future possibility; visualize a potential outcome.
ex: The founders envision a future where autonomous electric shuttles replace personal city vehicles.
nat: She envisions expanding the online training platform into Latin America next summer.

mis.bad: I envision to work remotely from Europe next year.
mis.good: I envision working remotely from Europe next year.
mis.why: Follow "envision" with a gerund ("-ing"), not an infinitive ("to work").

def: Lasting for a very short time; transient or fleeting.
ex: Fame gained from viral social media videos is usually ephemeral and quickly forgotten.
nat: Spring cherry blossoms have an ephemeral beauty that lasts only a few days.

mis.bad: Internet trends are very ephemerals in nature.
mis.good: Internet trends are very ephemeral in nature.
mis.why: English adjectives never take a plural "-s".

def: Heroic or grand in scale or character; exceptionally impressive.
ex: The development team concluded an epic six-month migration without any major production downtime.
nat: We watched an epic historical drama film at the film festival.

mis.bad: It was an epic adventure with many difficulties.
mis.good: It was an epic adventure despite the difficulties.
mis.why: Collocate "epic" directly with grand nouns like "journey", "scale", or "adventure".

def: A period of time in history or a person's life, typically marked by notable events.
ex: The mass commercialization of generative artificial intelligence clearly marks a new technological epoch.
nat: The industrial epoch transformed agricultural communities into crowded industrial cities.

mis.bad: We live in an epoch of great informations.
mis.good: We live in an epoch of great technological change.
mis.why: Remember "information" is uncountable, and "epoch" pairs naturally with "technological change" or "discovery".

def: Being the same in quantity, size, degree, or value.
ex: Every applicant must be given an equal opportunity to interview for the job opening.
nat: Dividing the company profits into equal shares satisfied all four founding partners.

mis.bad: Men and women must be treated equal in work.
mis.good: Men and women must be treated equally at work.
mis.why: Use the adverb "equally" to modify a verb, and "at work" for the location.

def: The state of being equal, especially in status, rights, and opportunities.
ex: The progressive organization campaigns tirelessly for gender equality and equal pay in technology.
nat: Racial equality remains a fundamental civil rights objective around the globe.

mis.bad: We must promote the equality between all workers.
mis.good: We must promote equality among all workers.
mis.why: Use "equality among [more than two]" and omit "the" when speaking generally about equality.

def: To consider one thing to be the same as or equivalent to another.
ex: One should never equate working long hours with being productive or truly effective.
nat: Many people incorrectly equate high price tags with superior product quality.

mis.bad: Do not equate high salary to happiness.
mis.good: Do not equate high salary with happiness.
mis.why: The standard collocation is "equate A with B", not "to".

def: A state in which opposing forces or influences are balanced.
ex: After weeks of market volatility, tech stock prices finally reached a stable economic equilibrium.
nat: Yoga and meditation help restore mental equilibrium after periods of severe stress.

mis.bad: The market stayed in an equilibrium balance.
mis.good: The market reached an equilibrium.
mis.why: Do not say "equilibrium balance"; "equilibrium" already means a state of balance.

def: To supply with the necessary items for a particular purpose or task.
ex: The company will equip all remote engineers with ergonomic chairs and high-resolution monitors.
nat: Practical speaking workshops equip students with confidence for job interviews abroad.

mis.bad: The laboratory is equipped by modern computers.
mis.good: The laboratory is equipped with modern computers.
mis.why: Always use "equipped with [tools/gear]", not "by".

def: Fair and impartial; dealing fairly and equally with all concerned.
ex: The board introduced an equitable distribution model for annual employee stock option grants.
nat: Access to clean drinking water should be equitable across all city districts.

mis.bad: We need an equitable solution for everyone involved.
mis.good: We need an equitable solution for all parties involved.
mis.why: Use "equitable" for fair sharing of resources or justice among parties.

def: Equal in value, amount, function, or meaning to something else.
ex: Completing this advanced cybersecurity course is equivalent to two full years of experience.
nat: Send ten dollars or the equivalent amount in your local currency.

mis.bad: This degree is equivalent with a master's degree.
mis.good: This degree is equivalent to a master's degree.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "to" after "equivalent": "equivalent to".

def: To destroy completely; put an end to something undesirable or harmful.
ex: Global health agencies have worked tirelessly for decades to eradicate infectious diseases completely.
nat: Good hygiene protocols can eradicate bacteria from hospital operating rooms.

mis.bad: The government tried to eradicate of corruption.
mis.good: The government tried to eradicate corruption.
mis.why: "Eradicate" is a transitive verb; do not add "of" after it.

def: To rub out or remove writing, recorded data, or painful memories.
ex: Be careful not to erase the configuration files while cleaning up your disk.
nat: Time alone could not erase the painful memories of the accident.

mis.bad: I erased the file by mistake from my computer.
mis.good: I erased the file from my computer by mistake.
mis.why: Place adverbial phrases like "by mistake" at the end of the sentence.

def: To gradually wear away soil, stone, or gradually destroy rights or confidence.
ex: High monthly inflation rates will erode consumer purchasing power across the entire economy.
nat: Ocean waves constantly erode the sandy cliffs along the southern coastline.

mis.bad: Inflation erodes of our savings over time.
mis.good: Inflation erodes our savings over time.
mis.why: "Erode" is transitive; do not use "of" after the verb.

def: Wrong; incorrect or based on mistaken beliefs or invalid data.
ex: The financial projection was based on completely erroneous assumptions about consumer demand growth.
nat: Investigators quickly dismissed the erroneous witness statements from the accident report.

mis.bad: His conclusion was totally erroneous in the report.
mis.good: His conclusion was totally erroneous.
mis.why: Collocate "erroneous" with "assumption", "belief", "data", or "conclusion".

def: To break free from confinement or control, or avoid danger or notice.
ex: The clever software engineer managed to escape the meeting before questions began.
nat: Two dangerous convicts escaped from the maximum-security prison last night.

mis.bad: He escaped from the fine because he was polite.
mis.good: He escaped a fine because he was polite.
mis.why: When meaning avoid a penalty or harm, use "escape + noun" without "from".

def: Cloth or other material produced by weaving or knitting fibers; or basic structure.
ex: The breathable cotton fabric helps athletes stay cool and comfortable during intense training sessions.
nat: Trust among teammates forms the very fabric of our company culture.

mis.bad: My father works in a car fabric.
mis.good: My father works in an automobile factory.
mis.why: False friend! "Fabric" means tecido or structure; a place where things are manufactured is a "factory".

def: To invent or concoct something, typically with deceitful intent; or construct an industrial item.
ex: The dishonest employee attempted to fabricate false receipts to claim unauthorized business travel expenses.
nat: Specialized workshops fabricate custom aluminum frames for solar panels.

mis.bad: He fabricated an excuse to not come.
mis.good: He fabricated an excuse for not coming.
mis.why: Use "excuse for not coming" or "excuse not to come".

def: Extraordinarily good or wonderful; or resembling a fable.
ex: We spent a fabulous afternoon exploring the historic cobblestone streets of old Lisbon.
nat: The company achieved fabulous financial returns during its first year in operation.

mis.bad: We had a fabulous time in our travel.
mis.good: We had a fabulous time on our trip.
mis.why: Collocate "on our trip", not "in our travel".

def: The front of a building; or an outward appearance maintained to conceal a less pleasant reality.
ex: Behind his cheerful and confident facade, the startup founder hid immense anxiety and exhaustion.
nat: The historic museum facade was restored using traditional lime mortar.

mis.bad: He showed a false facade of happiness.
mis.good: He maintained a facade of happiness.
mis.why: Collocate with verbs like "maintain", "put on", or "hide behind a facade".

def: To gradually grow faint and disappear, or lose color or brightness.
ex: Direct summer sunlight will cause brightly colored curtain fabrics to fade over several months.
nat: The applause began to fade as the speaker stepped up to the microphone.

mis.bad: The memory faded out from my mind.
mis.good: The memory faded from my mind.
mis.why: Say "fade from memory" or "fade away", not "fade out from".

def: Barely perceptible to the senses; weak or dizzy.
ex: The technician heard a faint clicking sound coming from inside the broken laptop casing.
nat: She felt dizzy and faint after skipping both breakfast and lunch.

mis.bad: I heard a weak noise downstairs late at night.
mis.good: I heard a faint noise downstairs late at night.
mis.why: Use "faint" rather than "weak" to describe barely audible sounds or faint lights.

def: Impartial and just treatment or behavior without favoritism or discrimination.
ex: Employees appreciated the total fairness with which the manager allocated flexible remote shifts.
nat: In all fairness, both candidates performed remarkably well during the final round.

mis.bad: The boss acted with fairness for everyone.
mis.good: The boss treated everyone with fairness.
mis.why: Collocate "with fairness" with verbs of treatment: "treated everyone with fairness / fairly".

def: Remaining loyal and steadfast; or accurately copying an original.
ex: The movie adaptation remained remarkably faithful to the original plot of the classic novel.
nat: Our dog has been a faithful companion through ten years of city life.

mis.bad: He remained faithful with his core values.
mis.good: He remained faithful to his core values.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "to" after "faithful": "faithful to something/someone".

def: Not genuine; imitation or counterfeit intended to deceive.
ex: Cybersecurity analysts warned users not to enter personal passwords on fake banking login pages.
nat: He bought a fake designer watch at a tourist night market.

mis.bad: He presented a falsified document (or "faked").
mis.good: He presented a fake / forged document.
mis.why: Use "fake" or "forged" as the natural adjective before nouns like document or passport.

def: A mistaken belief, especially one based on unsound argument or invalid reasoning.
ex: Believing that more developers on a delayed project will accelerate delivery is a fallacy.
nat: The philosopher dismantled the opponent's argument by exposing a fundamental logical fallacy.

mis.bad: That idea is a complete fallacy thought.
mis.good: That idea is a complete fallacy.
mis.why: "Fallacy" is a noun meaning false belief; do not combine it redundantly with "thought".

def: To alter or make false, especially so as to deceive; tamper with.
ex: The rogue accountant was arrested after attempting to falsify quarterly tax records repeatedly.
nat: A scientific hypothesis must be testable so that future experiments could potentially falsify it.

mis.bad: He tried to false the financial report.
mis.good: He tried to falsify the financial report.
mis.why: "False" is an adjective; the corresponding verb in English is "falsify".

def: To start to lose strength or momentum; speak or move hesitantly.
ex: Despite intense questioning from journalists, her voice did not falter for a single second.
nat: Economic growth began to falter following unexpected hikes in commercial lending interest rates.

mis.bad: Her courage faltered away during the interview.
mis.good: Her courage faltered during the interview.
mis.why: Do not add "away" to "falter"; use the verb simply as "falter".

def: Extreme scarcity of food causing widespread starvation across a geographical region.
ex: Severe drought and regional armed conflict combined to threaten millions of civilians with famine.
nat: International aid organizations rushed emergency supplies to relieve the catastrophic famine.

mis.bad: There is a big famine in the countryside.
mis.good: There is widespread famine in the countryside.
mis.why: Collocate "famine" with adjectives like "widespread" or "severe", rather than "big".

def: Known about by many people; renowned.
ex: The coastal Italian city is famous for its colorful cliffside houses and fresh seafood.
nat: She dreamed of becoming a famous software innovator known across the world.

mis.bad: The author is famous by his mystery novels.
mis.good: The author is famous for his mystery novels.
mis.why: Always use "famous for [an achievement]", never "by".

def: A person filled with excessive and single-minded zeal, or a passionate enthusiast.
ex: Our lead mobile developer is a fitness fanatic who cycles twenty miles every morning.
nat: Political fanatics rarely listen to opposing viewpoints with an open and fair mind.

mis.bad: He is a fanatic of football matches.
mis.good: He is a football fanatic.
mis.why: Place the subject directly before "fanatic" as a compound noun: "fitness fanatic", "football fanatic".

def: Overimaginative and unrealistic; existing only in imagination.
ex: The initial startup pitch included several fanciful projections that seasoned investors quickly dismissed.
nat: Children love stories set in fanciful worlds where animals speak and fly.

mis.bad: He wears a fanciful costume for carnival.
mis.good: He wears a colorful / whimsical costume for carnival.
mis.why: "Fanciful" means unrealistic or imaginative in concept, not elaborate in clothing ("costume").

def: Extremely interesting and charming; captivating.
ex: The documentary provided a fascinating look into how deep-sea creatures survive extreme water pressures.
nat: Quantum computing is a fascinating field that merges physics with advanced computer science.

mis.bad: I was very fascinating by the presentation.
mis.good: I was very fascinated by the presentation.
mis.why: Use "-ing" for the thing that causes interest ("fascinating talk") and "-ed" for the person feeling it ("fascinated").

def: A popular trend, especially in styles of dress; or a manner of doing something.
ex: The software team answered user inquiries in a prompt and highly organized fashion.
nat: Sustainable fashion brands are gaining popularity among environmentally conscious millennial shoppers.

mis.bad: She always dresses in the fashion.
mis.good: She always dresses in fashion / fashionable clothes.
mis.why: Say "in fashion" (trendy) or "fashionably", not "in the fashion".

def: To close or join securely, especially a belt, button, or gate.
ex: Flight attendants reminded all passengers to fasten their seatbelts before the plane departed.
nat: Fasten the screws tightly so the metal bracket cannot shake loose.

mis.bad: Please fasten up your seatbelt now.
mis.good: Please fasten your seatbelt now.
mis.why: Do not add "up" after "fasten"; note also the silent "t" (/ˈfæsn/).

def: Causing death; or leading to complete failure or disaster.
ex: Ignoring software security vulnerabilities can prove fatal to a startup's commercial survival.
nat: The reckless driver miraculously walked away unharmed from the fatal highway collision.

mis.bad: He had a fatal accident and went to hospital.
mis.good: He had a serious accident and went to hospital.
mis.why: If someone went to the hospital and survived, it was NOT fatal! "Fatal" strictly means causing death.

def: Extreme tiredness resulting from mental or physical exertion or illness.
ex: Software engineers often experience severe eye fatigue after staring at screens all afternoon.
nat: Decision fatigue makes it much harder to choose healthy options after work.

mis.bad: I felt a lot of fatigue after the run.
mis.good: I felt severe fatigue / felt fatigued after the run.
mis.why: Say "felt fatigued" or "suffered from fatigue" rather than "felt a lot of fatigue".

def: Responsibility for an accident or misfortune; or an imperfection in a system.
ex: The system crashed due to a technical fault in the legacy database synchronization script.
nat: It was completely my fault that the meeting started fifteen minutes late.

mis.bad: It is not my guilt that the bus was late.
mis.good: It is not my fault that the bus was late.
mis.why: False friend! "Guilt" is the moral feeling of culpability; use "fault" for responsibility for an error.

def: Working incorrectly or having defects; imperfect.
ex: The technician replaced the faulty memory module, which immediately resolved all server crashes.
nat: The entire argument collapsed because it rested on faulty economic premises.

mis.bad: The charger was with defect.
mis.good: The charger was faulty / defective.
mis.why: Avoid literal translation "with defect"; use the adjective "faulty" or "defective".

def: An achievement that requires great courage, skill, or strength.
ex: Building an operating system kernel from scratch is an extraordinary feat of engineering.
nat: Running an ultramarathon across the desert was an unforgettable physical feat.

mis.bad: Winning the prize was an heroic fact.
mis.good: Winning the prize was a heroic feat.
mis.why: False friend! Portuguese "feito" (accomplishment/deed) translates to English "feat", not "fact".

def: Savagely fierce, cruel, or violent; extreme and unpleasant.
ex: The island was battered by ferocious winds and torrential rain throughout the entire night.
nat: Tech companies face ferocious competition when recruiting senior artificial intelligence researchers.

mis.bad: The dog made a ferocious bark at us.
mis.good: The dog barked ferociously at us.
mis.why: Use the adverb "ferociously" to describe the action of barking or attacking.

def: Having or displaying a passionate intensity of feeling or belief.
ex: She is a fervent advocate for open-source software and transparent online privacy standards.
nat: The charity expressed fervent hopes that peace talks would succeed this week.

mis.bad: He has a fervent desire for to travel.
mis.good: He has a fervent desire to travel.
mis.why: Use "desire to + base verb", not "for to".

def: Cheerful and jolly; suitable for a festival or celebratory holiday.
ex: The historic downtown plaza took on a festive atmosphere with thousands of glittering lights.
nat: We enjoyed a wonderful festive dinner with friends on Christmas Eve.

mis.bad: The office was in a very festive ambient.
mis.good: The office had a very festive atmosphere.
mis.why: Do not use "ambient" for environment/vibe; use "festive atmosphere" or "festive mood".

def: To go for and bring back someone or something; or sell for a specified price.
ex: Could you please fetch me the blue notebook sitting on my office desk?
nat: The rare first-edition book is expected to fetch thousands at the auction.

mis.bad: I went to search my jacket from the car.
mis.good: I went to fetch my jacket from the car.
mis.why: Use "fetch" (go and bring back) rather than literal "search" when you know where the item is.

def: A prolonged and bitter quarrel, dispute, or state of conflict between parties.
ex: A bitter legal feud between the two patent holders delayed the product release.
nat: The historical feud between the rival families lasted for nearly a century.

mis.bad: They had a long fight that feud them.
mis.good: They were caught in a long feud.
mis.why: Use "feud" as a noun with verbs like "have a feud" or "be locked in a feud".

def: Dietary material that resists digestion; a thread of material; or optical fiber.
ex: Eating meals rich in dietary fiber helps maintain healthy digestion and steady blood sugar.
nat: High-speed fiber internet has been installed throughout the entire suburban neighborhood.

mis.bad: The doctor recommended eating more fibers.
mis.good: The doctor recommended eating more fiber.
mis.why: When referring to dietary roughage, "fiber" is uncountable in English.

def: Relating to or occurring in fiction; invented rather than true.
ex: Sherlock Holmes is perhaps the most famous fictional detective in modern English literature.
nat: The novel is set in a fictional kingdom on the Mediterranean coast.

mis.bad: The detective is a fiction character.
mis.good: The detective is a fictional character.
mis.why: Use the adjective form "fictional" before nouns like character, world, or town.

def: In a savagely violent, aggressive, or intensely determined manner.
ex: Global technology companies compete fiercely to attract the best machine learning research engineers.
nat: The local residents fought fiercely to preserve their historic neighborhood park.

mis.bad: They competed very fierce for the contract.
mis.good: They competed fiercely for the contract.
mis.why: Use the adverb "fiercely" to modify verbs such as "compete", "fight", or "protect".

def: Consisting of fire, or having a passionate, quick-tempered nature or spicy taste.
ex: The young opposition politician delivered a fiery speech against corporate tax loopholes yesterday.
nat: This traditional Mexican chili sauce has a fiery kick that surprises tourists.

mis.bad: The sauce is very fired.
mis.good: The sauce is very fiery / hot.
mis.why: Do not say "fired" (which means dismissed from a job); the adjective for spicy/blazing is "fiery".

def: To complete or settle the remaining details of an arrangement or agreement.
ex: The legal teams worked late into the night to finalize the acquisition contract.
nat: We should finalize our holiday travel itinerary before ticket prices rise again.

mis.bad: We need to finalize about the contract terms.
mis.good: We need to finalize the contract terms.
mis.why: "Finalize" is transitive; do not insert "about" after the verb.

def: Solid and unyielding to pressure; or strongly established and resolute.
ex: The company maintains a firm policy against sharing user data with outside advertisers.
nat: Make sure you have a firm grip on the handlebars while riding.

mis.bad: He gave me a very firmly handshake.
mis.good: He gave me a very firm handshake.
mis.why: Use the adjective "firm" to describe nouns like "handshake" or "decision".

pt: em primeira mão / direto da fonte
def: Coming directly from original observation or personal experience; direct.
ex: Living abroad gives professionals firsthand experience navigating unfamiliar cultural and business environments.
nat: She gave the police a firsthand account of the bank robbery.

mis.bad: I have experience in first hand with this issue.
mis.good: I have firsthand experience with this issue.
mis.why: Use the compound adjective "firsthand" before nouns: "firsthand experience", not "in first hand".

def: Relating to government or corporate revenue, taxation, and public spending.
ex: The corporation reported higher net profits during the third quarter of the fiscal year.
nat: Tight fiscal policy helped reduce government deficits across the euro area.

mis.bad: He works as a fiscal inspector in taxes.
mis.good: He works as a tax auditor / inspector.
mis.why: In Portuguese "fiscal" can be a noun (inspector/auditor); in English "fiscal" is strictly an adjective relating to budgets/taxes.

def: In good physical health, especially because of regular physical exercise.
ex: Running three times a week helped him stay remarkably fit and energized throughout winter.
nat: The doctor confirmed she was physically fit to run the marathon.

mis.bad: These shoes do not suit me well (meaning wrong size).
mis.good: These shoes do not fit me well.
mis.why: "Fit" refers to size/measurements; "suit" refers to style or appropriateness.

def: Suitable or appropriate under the given circumstances.
ex: A standing ovation was a fitting tribute to her thirty years of outstanding teaching.
nat: It seems fitting that the conference opens on International Women's Day.

mis.bad: It was a fittingly celebration for the team.
mis.good: It was a fitting celebration for the team.
mis.why: Use the adjective "fitting" before a noun, not the adverb "fittingly".

def: A piece of equipment fixed in position; or an established regular event.
ex: The annual international design summit has become a permanent fixture on our team calendar.
nat: The plumber installed new brass fixtures in both upstairs guest bathrooms.

mis.bad: The lights fixtures were broken in the room.
mis.good: The light fixtures were broken in the room.
mis.why: When used as an adjective modifying "fixtures", use singular "light": "light fixtures".

def: Conspicuously and outrageously bad, offensive, or reprehensible.
ex: Leaking sensitive customer credit card details constitutes a flagrant violation of global privacy laws.
nat: The referee showed an immediate red card for the player's flagrant foul.

mis.bad: He was caught in flagrant with the money.
mis.good: He was caught red-handed with the money.
mis.why: False friend! In Portuguese "em flagrante" translates to "caught red-handed", not "in flagrant".

def: A small, flat, very thin piece of something, typically one that has broken off.
ex: Delicate white snow flakes drifted softly through the cold mountain air all morning.
nat: Dry wall paint was peeling off in large thin flakes.

mis.bad: Dry skin was coming out in flakes of skin.
mis.good: Dry skin was flaking off.
mis.why: Use the verb "flake off" or simply say "peeling in flakes".

def: Tending to attract attention because of their exuberance, confidence, and stylish color.
ex: The famous singer was known worldwide for his flamboyant costumes and energetic stage performances.
nat: She brought a flamboyant personality to an otherwise quiet academic department.

mis.bad: His clothes were very flamboyants.
mis.good: His clothes were very flamboyant.
mis.why: Adjectives never take a plural "-s" in English.

def: A hot glowing body of ignited gas that is generated by something on fire.
ex: The flickering candle flame cast long dancing shadows across the wooden living room walls.
nat: Firefighters worked courageously to prevent the flames from spreading to nearby buildings.

mis.bad: The building caught in flames quickly.
mis.good: The building burst into flames / went up in flames.
mis.why: The idiomatic expressions are "burst into flames" or "go up in flames", not "caught in flames".

def: To burn with a sudden intensity, or suddenly erupt in violence or emotion.
ex: Tensions flared between union leaders and corporate management during the prolonged wage negotiations.
nat: The campfire flared brightly when dry pine needles were added.

mis.bad: Tensions flared up themselves during the meeting.
mis.good: Tensions flared up during the meeting.
mis.why: "Flare up" is intransitive; do not use a reflexive pronoun ("themselves").

def: A sudden brief burst of bright light or a sudden realization.
ex: A brilliant flash of lightning illuminated the entire dark mountain valley for one second.
nat: In a flash of inspiration, she finally solved the elusive coding puzzle.

mis.bad: The lightning made a big flash of light.
mis.good: There was a bright flash of lightning.
mis.why: Collocate "flash of lightning" naturally; avoid "made a big flash".

def: To praise someone lavishly, often insincerely, or make someone appear attractive.
ex: The junior executive tried to flatter the chief executive by laughing at every joke.
nat: That dark tailored jacket really flatters your shoulders and posture.

mis.bad: I was very flattering with your invitation.
mis.good: I was very flattered by your invitation.
mis.why: Use "-ed" for feelings ("I was flattered") and "-ing" for actions/things ("a flattering dress").

def: To display something ostentatiously, especially in order to provoke envy or admiration.
ex: He liked to flaunt his luxury sports car and designer watches in front of colleagues.
nat: True leaders demonstrate quiet confidence rather than flaunting their executive authority.

mis.bad: He flaunted about his new sports car.
mis.good: He flaunted his new sports car.
mis.why: "Flaunt" is transitive; do not insert "about" after it.

def: A mark, fault, or other imperfection that mars a substance or system.
ex: A critical security flaw was discovered in the third-party open-source encryption library today.
nat: The diamond was significantly cheaper because of a microscopic internal flaw.

mis.bad: There is a flaw on the program code.
mis.good: There is a flaw in the program code.
mis.why: Use the preposition "in" with "flaw": "a flaw in the code/system".

def: Without any blemishes, defects, or errors; completely perfect.
ex: Her English pronunciation and natural rhythm during the keynote address were almost flawless.
nat: The gymnastics champion delivered a flawless routine on the balance beam.

mis.bad: She gave a flawlessly performance on stage.
mis.good: She gave a flawless performance on stage.
mis.why: Use the adjective "flawless" before a noun like "performance".

def: A group of ships, airplanes, or motor vehicles operating together under the same ownership.
ex: The delivery startup replaced its entire commercial fleet with zero-emission electric cargo vans.
nat: The naval fleet conducted joint maritime security maneuvers across the Baltic Sea.

mis.bad: The company owns a fleet of car.
mis.good: The company owns a fleet of cars / vehicles.
mis.why: Use plural nouns after "fleet of": "fleet of cars", "fleet of aircraft".

def: Lasting for only a very short time; brief.
ex: He caught only a fleeting glimpse of the deer before it leaped into the forest.
nat: Childhood is a fleeting phase, so cherish every moment with your young kids.

mis.bad: Happiness was only a fleetingly feeling for him.
mis.good: Happiness was only a fleeting feeling for him.
mis.why: Use the adjective "fleeting" before nouns, not "fleetingly".

def: The soft substance consisting of muscle and fat that forms part of the body.
ex: The surgeon carefully examined the damaged flesh around the deep laceration before stitching.
nat: The juicy mango has sweet, aromatic orange flesh surrounding the flat seed.

mis.bad: I bought two pounds of bovine flesh at the butcher.
mis.good: I bought two pounds of beef at the butcher.
mis.why: Do not use "flesh" for meat you eat; use "meat", "beef", "chicken", or "pork".

def: Capable of bending easily without breaking; or ready and able to adapt to changes.
ex: Offering flexible working hours helps tech companies attract and retain experienced working parents.
nat: Silicon tubing is heat-resistant and extremely flexible for chemical laboratories.

mis.bad: My manager is very flexible with the times.
mis.good: My manager is very flexible about working hours.
mis.why: Use "flexible about" or "flexible with rules/hours".

def: To shine with an unsteady or wavering light; flutter rapidly.
ex: The fluorescent light in the office hallway started to flicker whenever someone walked by.
nat: A flicker of hope reappeared when rescue teams reached the remote mountain village.

mis.bad: The monitor flickered on and off continuously.
mis.good: The monitor flickered continuously.
mis.why: Say "flickered continuously" or "kept flickering"; "on and off" is redundant with "flicker".

def: To throw or hurl forcefully, casually, or carelessly.
ex: After working twelve straight hours, he flung his heavy backpack onto the living room couch.
nat: She flung open the heavy wooden shutters to let in the morning sunlight.

mis.bad: He flinged his coat on the chair.
mis.good: He flung his coat onto the chair.
mis.why: Irregular past tense: fling — flung — flung.

def: To turn over with a quick movement, or toss a coin.
ex: Let us flip a coin to decide who gives the opening conference presentation.
nat: He flipped through the textbook to review key grammar concepts before the exam.

mis.bad: She fliped the page of the magazine.
mis.good: She flipped the page of the magazine.
mis.why: Double the consonant when adding -ed or -ing: "flipped", "flipping".

def: To rest or move on or near the surface of a liquid without sinking.
ex: Hot air balloons float gently over the dramatic rock valleys of Cappadocia at sunrise.
nat: Oil floats on water because its physical density is lower than water density.

mis.bad: The wood was floating in top of the lake.
mis.good: The wood was floating on top of the lake.
mis.why: Use "on top of", not "in top of".

def: A number of birds or domestic animals of one kind feeding or resting together.
ex: A large flock of migratory birds flew south across the clear autumn sky yesterday.
nat: Tourists flock to the historic beach town every summer to enjoy warm weather.

mis.bad: We saw a group of birds flying south.
mis.good: We saw a flock of birds flying south.
mis.why: Use the specific collective noun "flock" for birds and sheep, rather than generic "group".

def: To grow or develop in a healthy or vigorous way, especially as the result of a particularly favorable environment.
ex: Independent coffee shops and bookshops flourish in this vibrant, walkable university neighborhood.
nat: Her confidence flourished after receiving constructive feedback from the engineering director.

mis.bad: Small businesses are flourishing very well here.
mis.good: Small businesses are flourishing here.
mis.why: Do not say "flourishing very well"; "flourish" already means develop very well.

def: Able to express oneself easily, smoothly, and articulately in a language.
ex: She became remarkably fluent in Portuguese after living and working in São Paulo for two years.
nat: Being fluent in English opens up international remote work opportunities for global software developers.

mis.bad: He speaks a very fluent English.
mis.good: He speaks fluent English / is fluent in English.
mis.why: Say "speaks fluent English" without "a", or "is fluent in English".

def: Soft fibers from fabrics or feathers that accumulate; or superficial trivial matter.
ex: Use a sticky lint roller to remove white cat fluff from your dark navy suit.
nat: The initial draft was thirty percent informative content and seventy percent corporate fluff.

mis.bad: Please remove the pelugem from the sofa.
mis.good: Please remove the fluff / lint from the sofa.
mis.why: Use "fluff" or "lint" for soft fibers that stick to clothes and furniture.

def: A substance that has no fixed shape and yields easily to external pressure.
ex: Doctors advise drinking plenty of fluids like warm tea and electrolyte water when sick.
nat: Brake fluid levels must be inspected regularly to maintain vehicle stopping performance.

mis.bad: Drink many fluids when you have a cold.
mis.good: Drink plenty of fluids when you have a cold.
mis.why: Collocate "plenty of fluids" or "lots of fluids", rather than "many fluids".

def: An unlikely chance occurrence, especially a surprising piece of luck.
ex: Winning the regional coding competition on his first try was definitely not a lucky fluke.
nat: Their first viral video was a complete fluke that happened by pure accident.

mis.bad: It was by a fluke that we won.
mis.good: It was a fluke that we won.
mis.why: Use "it was a fluke" directly as a noun predicate, not "by a fluke".

def: To cleanse by causing water to pass through; clear cache data; or blush red.
ex: Developers should flush the Redis cache whenever deploying breaking updates to user profile schemas.
nat: Her cheeks flushed red with embarrassment when her microphone unmuted unexpectedly.

mis.bad: Remember of flush the toilet.
mis.good: Remember to flush the toilet.
mis.why: Follow "remember" with an infinitive for duties: "remember to flush".

def: To bend something over on itself so that one part covers another.
ex: Please fold the clean laundry neatly before placing it inside the bedroom wardrobe.
nat: He sat quietly with his arms folded while listening to the keynote lecture.

mis.bad: He doblated the paper in half.
mis.good: He folded the paper in half.
mis.why: The English verb is "fold", not a Portuguese loanword.

def: Having an affection or liking for someone or something; foolishly affectionate.
ex: I have very fond memories of spending summer vacations at my grandparents' farm.
nat: She is extremely fond of classical piano music and attends concerts regularly.

mis.bad: I am very fond for Italian cooking.
mis.good: I am very fond of Italian cooking.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "of" after "fond": "fond of something".

def: Lacking good sense or judgment; unwise and imprudent.
ex: It would be foolish to deploy unverified database migrations directly to the live server.
nat: He felt foolish when he realized he had worn mismatched shoes to work.

mis.bad: It was a fool mistake to click that phishing link.
mis.good: It was a foolish mistake to click that phishing link.
mis.why: Use the adjective "foolish" before nouns; "fool" is a noun.

def: An ancillary piece of information printed at the bottom of a page.
ex: Always consult the explanatory footnote at the bottom of the table for calculation definitions.
nat: The scandal will likely become just a brief footnote in the company's long history.

mis.bad: Check the footnote on the bottom of the page.
mis.good: Check the footnote at the bottom of the page.
mis.why: Use "at the bottom of the page", not "on".

def: Recorded film material or video representing a specific event.
ex: The police reviewed hours of security camera footage to identify the suspect vehicle.
nat: Documentary filmmakers captured extraordinary drone footage of the erupting Icelandic volcano.

mis.bad: They showed many footages of the accident.
mis.good: They showed hours of footage / a lot of footage of the accident.
mis.why: "Footage" is uncountable in English; do not pluralize to "footages".
